utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosector versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It should be noted for the transcript that Judge Robinson is back with us today; however, he will have to be absent for some time next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on in accordance with the summary, there were some photographs which weren't available yesterday but are available today to help. May they be distributed as a group of four black and white photocopies for the Bench, and may the originals in due course go onto the ELMO. And if the usher would take from me a plan that I've marked. And I hope nobody would object to it. It is a general indication. And lay the bit with the red markings on the ELMO so that it can be seen. A little bit further so that we can get the other one in as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness, please, have the colour photographs in sequence. Would you look at the first one. Put it on the ELMO, perhaps, so that everyone can see. Does that show the road leading up to the -- I've forgotten the name -- the villa, which was the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we take the photograph off and look at what I've marked. Just take the photograph off, please. I've marked as "1" in red -- you can't see it now. Yes, we can. There it is. Marked as "1", a place. Is it consistent with a view from that place looking up towards the villa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No. This is the villa. You can see part of the villa here [indicates]. And as for the view from the villa vis-a-vis --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am going to stop you. If you look at the position marked number "1" on the plan. Perhaps the usher would just point that out to you. Where I've marked a number "1," is the photograph consistent with having been taken from there, please? Your Honour, it wasn't possible to go through the photographs with this witness yesterday. They weren't yet developed. Can we --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: That's this part over here [indicates], the villa is here. It's marked over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: So it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we see here the villa with a balcony in front of it, and is that the view that you would get if standing in the position, roughly standing in the position marked "2," where the usher will point his finger on the plan? Number "2" is the view there. Roughly, what you would get from number "2" looking up to the villa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The villa is above number "2," that is to say above this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Right here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph number. Does this, and the following photograph -- and they may be laid side by side, I think, so that we can see them both together on the ELMO -- does this show a view down towards the three that we can see fish ponds used for the cultivation of salmon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: [Indicates] The photograph over here was taken from here, from this road. This is the fish pond, part of it. And up here are the buildings that were built subsequently, the rest homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I can return now to the summary. Thank you very much to the usher. Witness T, this morning we must move at a faster speed because of the requirements of other witnesses and so on. So I am going to ask you a number of questions which I hope you won't think it rude of me. I would like you to answer, if you can, simply yes or no, and then we'll move on that much more quickly. I am at paragraph 68. At about the -- in the summer of 1992, did you notice any soldiers coming from outside Busovaca? Just yes or no. And if the answer is yes --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- what did their insignia show them to be? What did their insignia show them to have come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: They did not wear any insignia, but their accents showed that they came from Herzegovina, the way they pronounced words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any other insignia at that stage indicating people coming from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No. [Realtime transcript read in error "Yes"].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes? Well, if it was yes, where from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: My assumption is that they were from Herzegovina. That's Grude, Siroki Brijeg, Mostar and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to turn now, first of all, to something that you can deal with very briefly. In October was there a conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in Novi Travnik, and by November of 1992 had the situation in Busovaca got worse, with looting and bombing of Muslim shops and with the HVO placing restrictions on the movements of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 71. On or about the 20th of January 1993, had you gone for coffee with a man called Mirsad Delija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your return, did you notice something of the movements of a particular motor car? If so, tell us the colour and what you saw of its licence plate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The vehicle was a white Golf and it had an HVO licence plate without any numbers, and there was a chequerboard sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did this vehicle do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: As we were moving from town towards the houses, we were stopped on two occasions from the direction of Ravne. At certain moments the lights would change; that is to say that they would light the road in different ways, to a greater or to a lesser extent, and they would pass by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many times did the vehicle pass you by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got to your house, did you invite Mirsad Delija to join you, but did he in fact go to his mother's house, his mother being alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At some time, perhaps 25 minutes later, did you hear firing and did you hear Mirsad's sister Zumetra screaming for help, in consequence of which did you go to Mirsad's house and find him on the ground, having been shot several times? Was he then taken to Zenica dying on the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just, please, yes or no to this question: Did you discuss this issue with Mirsad's brother Arif Delija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no: Did he tell you what had happened earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From what he told you, had he, Arif Delija, been personally present at the events that he was describing to you? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe my question needs further clarification. I don't want to know the detail of what Delija told you, but according to what he said, had he been present with his brother earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was he, Arif Delija, then able to tell you what his brother Mirsad had been doing that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why not, if he had been present with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: On that day, he was not with his brother Mirsad. He was with his other brother, Miralem Delija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And therefore what was the source of your information about what had happened to Mirsad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: From his brother Arif Delija, actually Mirsad had been killed in Busovaca in '92, '93, in January. Arif Delija belonged to the Territorial Defence in the local commune of Kacuni, so at that point in time, they had not been together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So for the duration -- as you understood it, for the totality of this day, who had been with Mirsad? Was it Miralem, or was it Arif, or was it both of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: On that day it was I, personally, who was with Mirsad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but earlier in the day, who had been with Mirsad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: None of his brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you've been asking about this for some time; I wonder if there is any point in pursuing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's obviously a very important piece of evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and it would be, of course, one of a number of pieces of evidence going to the overall issue, which we would invite you in due course to consider collectively, but Your Honour sees the difficulties that I presently encounter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I ask one question which I hope won't, as it were, go to the content, but will just give me a chance to establish the route of information; and then, if it's not satisfactory, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you, please, Witness T, to listen quite carefully to this question, and just to answer it in the precise way I invite you to do so, because it's to do with various rules we have in these courts. Don't tell us what was said to have happened at a particular place, for example a checkpoint, earlier in the day, but can you tell us the route by which you learnt the information? By that I mean, if you can explain that it was Mr. X who told Mr. Y, who then told you, or if it was simply Mr. X who told you. That's all I want to know: the route by which the information came to you. First of all, do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then can you tell me, please, or tell the Court, please, the route by which you learnt information of what happened at a particular checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I personally was told about this by Arif Delija in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Arif Delija had learnt it how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: From his brother Miralem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is either of those brothers still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No, not a single one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems it does come from one brother via another. In light of the death of both of those intervening witnesses, it is the only source of information available to us. We have already heard quite a lot of evidence surrounding this event; there may be further evidence confirmatory of the account given. In particular, if the Court looks at paragraph 75 and at what is said there in the second line, there is a named witness there who will be or may be coming to help us, and I'd ask the Court to admit the evidence on the usual basis that its weight can be considered at a later stage. To exclude it now would be to deny forever the chance of it being part of the overall evidential picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I was waiting for the end of the interpretation. I listened to all of this very carefully because I was afraid that the witness would be led to an answer, but I think it is quite clear now that it is double hearsay at the least. The Defence has no opportunity of checking this out from the person from which this witness heard about what had happened at this checkpoint, so our objection is that this is at least double hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit this evidence. We notice the criticisms which are made of it. The weight, of course, is something which we will have to determine. By itself, it would not be sufficient to draw any inference, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness T, will you tell us, please, what you learnt from the other two men, the brothers, about what had happened earlier that day at a certain checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Miralem Delija, who was at the Kacuni checkpoint then -- I mean, they stopped vehicles that were coming back from Kiseljak to Busovaca for the purpose of identification, in order to identify persons and passengers. Among others in these vehicles was Kordic. Then there was also Bozo Rajic, and there was Kostroman, a professor of chemistry from Vitez; in fact, the entire delegation of the HDZ which had had a meeting in Kiseljak. Miralem just wanted to record the fact that they had passed, and he wanted to see their IDs, and that was the duty of this checkpoint, and then he wanted to let them go. However, since they knew each other personally, Dario Kordic and Miralem Delija, Kordic insulted and humiliated both the checkpoint and the insignia that he wore and himself personally. He thought -- I mean Miralem thought that this was not right. With the other men there, he disarmed his escorts and the other men from the delegation and took them in the direction of the silos. About 30 or 40 minutes later, they were all released from the silos, with their weapons and with their vehicles, at the intervention and request of Husein Hadzimejlic and others who were then in command in the Territorial Defence, who insisted that they should be released, and in fact they were released. As they were leaving the checkpoint, because again this same delegation went by the same checkpoint, Dario Kordic said to Miralem Delija, in passing, that he would remember this well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Miralem and Mirsad live in the same house or in different houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: They lived in different houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long after the release of these men, as you understood it, was Mirsad killed at his house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: After leaving the checkpoint and after Dario Kordic's remark, no more than 45 minutes went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am now going to turn to questions that I think you will be able to deal with by yes/no answers. And I will be assisted if my friends opposite read a paragraph or so ahead and indicate when they want me to do otherwise. Is it right that the conflict between Muslims and Croats in Busovaca started on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but that was the open conflict. And by that I mean an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the morning of the 26th and 27th, starting at about 5.15, did the HVO go through Busovaca, both disarming and capturing Muslims, and was a man called Floro Glavocevic using a loudspeaker, instructing Muslims to surrender and turn over their arms, saying that HVO would guarantee their safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the commander of the local police, Ante Sliskovic, the commander of the military police, Vlado Cosic, and were you in fact not interrogated but taken to Kaonik Camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The commander of the civilian police was Kristo and the commander of the military police was Vlado Cosic. I was not interrogated. I was taken to the camp in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 81 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: With everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First, were you held in a hangar, some 10 metres by 60 metres, where your estimate is that there were some 380 prisoners and where you were detained for some three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 83. Did the HVO come to the hangar, read off lists of names of those to be interrogated on the grounds that they were alleged to have formed an Islamic municipality, and were others alleged to be extremist fundamentalists or commanders of Mujahedin units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear of others being used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of Muslim prisoners being taken, tied by a rope with about one metre between each man, to villages, where they would be sent in ahead of the HVO, who would come behind, equipped with weapons and loudspeakers, enforcing the surrender of local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of that clearance of villages happening at Skradno, Loncari, Strane and Rovna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 87. Between the 29th and 30th of January, or thereabouts, were new cells made and were you taken from the hangar and placed in those cells, each being some three by four metres in size and containing some 20 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were not beaten, but one of your brothers was. Please don't name him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you used to dig trenches at different locations, and in particular at Donja Solakovici, Kula and Skradno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The guards included a neighbour, whom you've named, but I won't identify. Did the guards inspire some fear in you, wearing paint on their faces and sometimes wearing black uniforms with swastikas on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 93. In the course of trench-digging, were two men, to your knowledge, killed: one, Nermin Elezovic, who went out -- paragraph 94 -- to the general area of Kula, where, under the direction of a former schoolmate, whom you've named, was that man, Elezovic, sent to an area of Donji Solakovici, where he was killed in a Croat house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, paragraphs 95 and 96 come in the source of information from others. I'm not going to pursue it in the setting of this case. 97. Was another prisoner, Sehovic, killed in the course of trench-digging that same night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Part of 97, really, is subject of a separate paragraph, but I'll deal with it. In the course of your time at Kaonik, did you see Sliskovic there at the time when prisoners were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a man named Cakara, who, as you understood it, left the camp, never to be seen alive again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the eventual exchange of prisoners, to your knowledge, did the defendant Kordic play any role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I can say that he must have known of everything that was going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 101. Was there one particular Muslim family, not necessarily now to be named, who was well-known to Kordic or to his family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that particular Muslim family the subject of different and preferential treatment throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they never lose their property nor, indeed, their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 104. On the exchange organised by the Red Cross, did you elect to return to Busovaca, and between the 25th of February and the 1st of April of 1993 was there an effective ceasefire between Croats and Muslims, and in the course of that ceasefire were Muslim -- or perhaps Muslim householders given a document signed by Kordic and Sliskovic which stated that non-Croats were under HVO protection in respect of property and possessions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court already has the document 861, I think. Yes, it's 861 and 861,1. Those can be shown briefly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we don't have -- or I don't appear to have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming up right now. It will be 861,1(a). If the English version translation can be placed on the ELMO, please. Well, perhaps not, because it identifies someone, but not this defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does the body of the statement read as translated into English? It's dated the 1st of May and it says: "Pursuant to demonstrated need, after finding that certain members of the Busovaca HVO units whose residential buildings had been destroyed in combat operations in the area of Busovaca municipality were trying to solve their existential problems by force, and with the aim of preventing such occurrences and protecting the safety of persons and property for all citizens, regardless of their political, religious and national affiliation, I hereby issue --" then there is the name of a resident, "-- of Busovaca the following certificate whereby it is forbidden to Busovaca HVO members to harass the above-named person and members of his family, threaten the safety of their person and property and take any wilful actions which would result in a threat to the safety of their person and property. The strictest measures envisaged by law shall be taken against the perpetrators." And the signature is not as I forecast, but the signatures are Grubesic, Maric and Kordic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to your personal version of such a certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: My copy, in fact the original, was torn up at a doorstep -- at my doorstep in Busovaca by masked, armed persons who were in the habit of coming on a daily basis to loot, taking money and gold, under the pretence that for them such certificates meant nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The version you produced, which has a neighbour's name on it, is similar to the copy that you have for yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this Exhibit please be under seal. Paragraph 108. Did, in your judgement, the mistreatment of Muslims continue between March and August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 111. Was a group of some 160 Muslims formed who were compelled to dig trenches in groups, the groups themselves being rotated in and out of trench-digging jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you used to dig trenches around Loncari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see some two Muslims killed in the course of trench-digging work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 109. Were you also used, between March and September, as a human shield at Strane, Kula and Komari? And Komari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you leave Busovaca late 1993, eventually going in the direction of Zenica, not returning to Busovaca since?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you produced to the Prosecution a wartime newspaper, or many pages from a wartime newspaper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you actually have the original with you this morning, or is it still back at the hotel room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I have it on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I've done here, in order to avoid burdening the Court with unnecessary paperwork, is I have had copied all of the newspaper for the Defence, and I've distributed it to them last night. It contains a number of articles, but locked within the articles are three orders and one photograph, and it's the orders and photograph that I wish to produce. I can do it swiftly, save for the fact that by my oversight, there is no official translation of the one order I may need to look at in detail. The Court should have, I hope, a small clutch of four documents that looks like this, an enlarged newspaper extract; and if the Court has those, from this newspaper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we haven't. We've merely got a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry; I don't know what's gone wrong, then, on that. The Defence were provided with them yesterday, and there's obviously something gone wrong with our distribution. No, those are the original documents as tendered. I see what's happened. I see what's happened. Can I make available to the usher for laying on the ELMO, please, a clutch of four documents which will be copied at the break and made available to the Court as already to the Defence. And if we look at them in the order in which they turn up, if the usher would be so good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, a comment on the documents which the Prosecutor is trying to tender. We received a copy of the newspapers which the witness has brought along last night. These are newspapers from July of 1993, and that newspaper was distributed only by the Muslim side. That is, that was a Muslim media outlet, very hostile towards the Croats, and that can be gleaned just by the perusal of the newspaper, where, in many places, instead of "Croats," the Croats are labelled as "Ustashas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We follow that. This is a comment about the weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was just a preliminary remark. Our objection is that we are not opposed to the introduction of the document regarding the establishment of Herceg-Bosna; we know about this document. But the document labelled as -- marked 248,2 is something we have not seen before, and we have grounds for doubting its veracity and authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What document are you speaking about? What is this really about, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The copy is marked Z248,2. This is what we received from the Prosecution last night. And I would like to point out to the Trial Chamber the last sentence, and I have never seen anything like that in any document ever produced by the Croatian side, which actually is the grounds for my questioning its authenticity. It would seem, on the basis of this document, that the command staff of the 1st Battalion had ordered that somebody be executed should they oppose or resist the carrying out of this order. And also there was another document introduced by the Prosecutor earlier, that was Z62, which obviously is a copy of one of the newspapers from the same bundle. As Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic, I can say that neither Mr. Kordic nor we as a team have any knowledge of this source, and given the source, this newspaper, we unfortunately have to question its veracity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's difficult to deal with these matters without a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and the document only came yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. It's difficult to deal, indeed, without translation. The documents only came yesterday, and the one document that I should have given absolute priority to translation, I failed to do, and all I've got is an on-sight translation. Can I explain, however, what the position is. There are three orders that are produced in the newspaper. Two of them have already been produced in either similar or identical formats already, and that would tend to show the reliability of the newspaper, at least in respect of those orders. The third order is not one that we have sourced from anywhere else. This is the best version, as it were, that we have of this document, true or false. We would invite it to be adduced now, weight for later. I'm sorry, "weight"; I mean the weight of the evidence obviously coming later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we find out where the witness got the newspaper from, and let's have a look at the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness T, can you produce, please, the original of the newspaper and show it to us, and can you tell us, please, where you obtained that newspaper from and in what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The circumstances which compelled me to ask for this newspaper is such that in these newspapers, a statement was given by an individual who witnessed the murder of my brother. So that was the reason why I looked for this newspaper, and the purpose was to locate the person who survived and who would give me a first-hand account on my brother. And in time, this corroborated the statements and reports which appeared in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it just so happened that the same edition of the newspaper, the original of which is probably quite valuable to you as a personal item, it just so happened that that newspaper also contained set out within it three orders and one photograph that we took copies of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, this is a newspaper. A newspaper remains a newspaper. As Mr. Nice said yesterday, we shouldn't forget that these are professional judges in front of you; we know what a newspaper is. We also know what a tendentious newspaper is. There's a certain orientation in this newspaper. We're not going to spend forever with this newspaper. It's worth what it's worth. It's a newspaper article. Now what we have to do is to have a translation of the article so we can at least know what's in it, but I don't think we have to spend forever speaking about this. The Prosecutor has brought in a newspaper article brought in by one of the witnesses; it's worth what it's worth. So we're still talking about the weight, as my colleague said a few minutes ago. That's what we're dealing with, and not with something which should take up the Tribunal's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let us return the newspaper to the witness. It may be sensible to adjourn now and try and get some translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have an unofficial draft translation. I know the rules of the Translation Unit here are properly strict, but if we can distribute that temporarily and if I can get the people in the booth simply to translate the last and, I understand, contentious passage at the witness's reading it, that may bring me to the end of this witness's examination-in-chief. Would that be a suitable course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the four sheets of paper be laid before the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, before we get to that point, you have to first tell us yourself why you have brought in that newspaper article. Perhaps that could help us. What is the interest of having brought that newspaper article in, other than the interest that the witness has just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Both for the third order, which we -- of which we don't have any sight independently. We have the first two; they're already produced -- and for the photograph that you'll see very shortly. So can you lay it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does the first order, or is the first order set out in the newspaper an order of the 21st of March, 1992, and the Court will know from its records, or I can inform it in due course, an order to the like effect has already been produced by another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 23rd of October, 1992, is a second order, again, already produced -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the one which is not produced. Can I distribute now, please, to the Court, some draft translations, and to Defence counsel. One more coming. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you mentioned the two other orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be helpful to know what their numbers are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. The first exhibit, the 23rd of March, was Exhibit 62, and it was produced on the 23rd of April of this year by an open witness, Cicak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what was it about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was a request for a meeting with Susak and setting out the attendance of various people. The other order that was produced is dated the 10th of April of 1992. It's Exhibit 71, and it was the establishment of the Croatian Defence Council. And so those two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are in the clip, actually. We have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this is the third one, and what I would invite the Chamber to do, bearing in mind that a proper translation will be forthcoming in due course, would be perhaps to read for themselves, rather than read into any part of the public record, an at-sight translation, and I will get the witness simply to read out the last passage, which is the particularly contentious passage so far as the Defence are concerned for purposes of any cross-examination. If the Chamber will be good enough to read it to themselves, they will see its potential significance, if a true document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, you're telling us that this document is authentic. Do you intend to show any proof that it is authentic? Or are you going to limit yourself to that press article?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the moment, having just myself seen the article for the first time yesterday because the witness brought the newspaper yesterday, I am producing it for what it is. It comes along with other orders that are apparently genuine, and our inquiries will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, speaking for myself, I would say that for the time being, we can understand that this type of document is something which comes from the newspaper, from the press, and with all reservations that that includes. It cannot be constituent of a document which has any kind of probative force in and of itself so long as it has not been confirmed in a more official manner, so long as there are no further elements to come to back it up. So as I said a few minutes ago, it remains something which comes from a newspaper, and that's what we will take it as.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Witness T, would you help us, please, to this extent. You see on the screen in front of you a document which has about two-thirds of the way down some underlining. Would you just read out, fairly slowly so that the translators can translate, the sentence that is underlined and -- yes, just that sentence, please, to start with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: "All members of the BiH Army should be disarmed --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Carry on, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: "-- disarmed, imprisoned, and eventually released after 24 hours. The Mujahedin should be liquidated and the other members of the Muslim forces should not be released pending further notice."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can you please look right at the bottom of the document, literally the last sentence that you can see there, please. Just read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: "The excerpt from this order is given on the basis of an order of the command of Central Bosnia from the 22nd of October 1992, on the basis of which public mobilisation was proclaimed for all men fit for military service. Members of the HVO who convincingly --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness has misread what the paper says, says the interpreter. The verb is not --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: "-- disarm." I can't see this. It's illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. A proper translation to be provided soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The exhibit number, please, of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The exhibit number of the whole clutch is 248,2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see the last sheet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Judges' microphones are on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The point is that, of course, at the moment we've got this unofficial translation and therefore it may be wrong to enter it as an exhibit. But we'll give it this number pending the official arrival, the official translation when it can be formally admitted. But until that time it's not an official exhibit; marked, Judge Robinson suggests, for identification. That would be a sensible way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And may the witness now see the last of the four sheets on this -- of the document that I placed before him, which is the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see from the same photograph -- I beg your pardon, from the same newspaper a photograph showing Kostroman, Kordic and Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can one see in full an arm patch bearing the insignia HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you see anything of an arm patch on the middle figure of the three, Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that is 248,2(a). Yes, wait there. You will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour. We'll sit again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would just like to put some numbers, right, of the exhibits. There was a document submitted yesterday by the OTP, which was marked 248,2. This was this newspaper article. So this is not yet admitted into evidence, but the unofficial draft translation will be numbered 248/2A. And the photograph will be numbered 248/2B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start, I would like to intervene on a certain point. I talked to my colleagues and we looked at the transcript. In response to a question on page 4 of today's transcript, line 24, the witness answered in Croat "no"; however, the transcript says "yes," and it should have been "no." So could the stenographers check this out with the interpreters later, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was put by the Prosecutor whether the witness saw insignia, insignia of persons who came out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the answer was -- and then the witness said from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So you can see from the sense of the sentence that the answer had to be "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what I recollect him saying. Yes, well that can be put right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, may I introduce myself. I am Mitko Naumovski. I am a defence attorney from Zagreb and I am one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Dario Kordic. I am going to put a few questions to you, but I have to tell you in advance something that is usually said. Since we understand each other full well when we start speaking, we should wait for the interpretation to come out in other languages. My first question, perhaps we could start with that, relates to what you heard had happened in Kacuni. First of all, I am not sure whether you said this. On which date did this occur in Kacuni; that is to say, when these persons were stopped at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The date, in all fairness, I do not know for sure, but I know that it was in January 1993, that is to say before the killing of Mirsad Delija. That is to say that it was during the night, according to the information that I received, in the afternoon, between 5.00 and 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not understand. Was it the same day or was it the day when Mirsad Delija was killed, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: It was the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I would agree with you that it was in the afternoon, around 4.00, if that's what you meant by afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, between 4.00 and -- well, it was January, night-time, early night-time. There was a fog and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said today for the first time that you heard about this event from Arif Delija only in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you were in contact with him before that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You saw him only then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I was in Busovaca from the 28th of January, 1993 until the 15th of September, 1993. Arif Delija was in the local commune of Kacuni; that is to say that we were on two different sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, he was a soldier in the 33rd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today you said this incident occurred at a point in time when several people were coming to Busovaca from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you mentioned their names; that is, Mr. Kordic, Mr. Kostroman, and a professor of chemistry, you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, Valentic (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Are you referring to Anto Valenta from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, I have to tell you that as you made two statements earlier on, you said that at that checkpoint only two men were stopped and searched at that checkpoint, that is to say Mr. Kordic and Blaskic. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: That's what I had heard. There is a possibility of Blaskic having been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are not sure that Blaskic was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But today you mentioned the name of Bozo Rajic for the first time. Are you sure that it was those people who you mentioned today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: This is the way it was. The gentlemen who were in the top leadership of the Croatian institutions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Sorry that I am interrupting --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: -- they held meetings every day, political meetings in the hall of the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I am sorry. I have to interrupt you. Please, could you answer the question that I put to you? And it's a very simple question. You mentioned a few persons today who were stopped at this checkpoint and you never mentioned them before, and you made two statements earlier on. And you mentioned General Blaskic, and you said that you were not sure whether he was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Why do you mention these persons for the first time today? A lot more time has gone by in the meantime. I mean, until today rather than until the day when you made your first statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, I was not there at the checkpoint, and the delegation had had a meeting in Kiseljak on that same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, that's your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. Opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you base this opinion and conclusion of yours upon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Conclusion? I base my opinion and conclusion on the assumption that these persons had a meeting in the municipality of Busovaca afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you're not sure of that; that's only your assumption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, that's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So what you told us today about what happened in Kacuni --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: -- I mean, the persons who were stopped, that is your assumption, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Among others, well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to put our position to the witness right now, and I don't want really to waste much time over this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, I have to tell you the pure truth, and that is that Mr. Kordic was not in Kacuni during those days at all, and he was not stopped at that checkpoint. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: That's your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, that's a fact. I'm going to tell you who was stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, it's the witness who gives evidence. You can make suggestions and put matters to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. The witness asked me, so I answered. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On that day, Mr. Kostroman and Mr. Blaskic were stopped, but they were going from Busovaca to Kiseljak, not the other way around. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: What about Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, please answer my question first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I did not know the direction. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now, my other question related to

utterances.speaker: MR. KORDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic did not leave Busovaca during those days at all. In view of your assumptions, the ones that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it is. My opinion is that some people were stopped there, and the assumption leads to one name at least. My source of information is almost accurate. The witnesses, unfortunately, all three brothers, all three Delija brothers, were killed. Somebody had issued an order after all to liquidate Mirsad Delija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, I have to interrupt you. The Defence never claimed that Mirsad Delija had not been killed. We are not claiming that. We are now talking about what happened in Kacuni at that checkpoint. If I understand your assumptions correctly, you actually do not know whether Mr. Kordic was there or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think -- just a moment, please. I think you've taken this as far as you can with the witness, Mr. Naumovski. You've put your case to him. The witness has told us what he heard and where he heard it from. He's not saying, of course, that he was there at the time. I don't think you can really take it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, the witness spoke of his assumptions, and then some names perhaps were mentioned involved in these assumptions and others were not, and he did not say which names were part of his assumptions. But if you believe that enough light has been thrown on this, then we may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So, Mr. T, I'll take you back to the beginning. You gave your first statement on 27 September 1996, to the Centre for Public Security in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you please say "yes," because nodding cannot be taken down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You also gave a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal at the end of January of this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you also perhaps give a statement to the agency for investigation of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the presidency? When did you give that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Perhaps in '95, '96.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Was a record taken? In other words, was it written down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you perhaps have that statement on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I thought that perhaps you had it, because we don't. You will agree with me that whenever you gave a statement on what you knew, you spoke to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You spoke about things that you knew to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I am a craftsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you still work as a craftsman today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where did you work in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I worked in the steelworks until '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And after that, were you employed, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I was laid off. I could not move and go to Zenica freely and could not go for medical care, since I had a leg injury, and I could not go there for my regular medical exams and for the disability commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You're talking about the period when thousands of Croats who lived in Busovaca, Vitez, and had worked in Zenica, were left jobless?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: At that time, both Croats and Muslims, a large number of those employed in the steelworks in Zenica had taken the two-year salary, and then some of them left Central Bosnia altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not dwell on that. When did you leave Busovaca? 1993, 1994? When was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Late 1993 is when I was mobilised in the ABiH, and I remained in the army until the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What unit were you in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mean 303rd, or 333rd?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That was in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it was in the territory of the Busovaca municipality, nevertheless?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in the course of 1992, you were a member of the Territorial Defence in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Along with Arif Delija and many other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, and many Croats, because a number of Croats were also members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell me, very briefly, let's go through the events which you gave evidence about when you went with Arif Delija, when you went fishing with him. Yesterday, in examination-in-chief, you said that when you went there in early July '92, that you were stopped at the checkpoint in Meraja, at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, as you come onto the bridge to get to Tisovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that you were advised that you had to go back, that you couldn't go on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that you still managed somehow to convince the soldiers to let you through, and they in turn told you that you were seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, they told us not to tell anybody that they had seen us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. We mentioned your previous statements, and I want to point out a detail to you. Earlier, on both occasions when you -- both on the occasion when you spoke to the ICTY investigators and to the Bosnian authorities, you said that you went around this checkpoint in order not to be seen by the soldiers because they would have barred you from passing through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, they pointed out and they advised us to go around this ground and to then go fishing and not to make reference to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. But you never said that before. And I am going to tell you why I am raising this as an important point, because on that occasion you said that you and Arif, on your own initiative, decided to go forth, and I quote you, "regardless of everything," and again I quote you, "at our own risk." So that would mean that not only did nobody let you pass, but you took it upon yourself to go at your own risk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out to you that this is not what you said yesterday and today, because what you said on this occasion is the exact opposite of what you had said before. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The truth is that we were warned and that we proceeded on -- on our own responsibility to go fishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you say that they let you go, that they let you pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Which is what you said yesterday for the first time. Now, tell me, why would you run the risk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: We did not see that we should have been prevented from fishing, because we went along the Ivancica River all the time and we kept -- we fished all the time. So we did not think it very dangerous to keep moving on in order to fish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Even in spite of the fact that you saw an improperly buried or hastily buried body of a soldier nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in that respect, just one question. You say that this body was buried up, so to speak, in the open, not somewhere where it's a hidden place, but right next to the bridge, so that certain parts of the bodies could even be seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You described the first incident. I am not going to repeat it, but let me ask you: You were basically accused of being infiltrated because you were in that area without permission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, when the situation was clarified, Grubesic escorted you back and, in essence, apologised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In late July you went towards the black top or the Mount Busovaca for the second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This is some 10, 15 kilometres away from Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Some two hours' walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And about, what, 10 or more kilometres away from Tisovac also, or the other way? I mean from the black summit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just give us an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: There were 15 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mean kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: With respect to the second incident, you gave two statements, which we referred to just now. And just in general, I don't want to go into detail, but in the first statement you described in detail that you saw the manner in which this one soldier whom you believed to have been a member of the Serbian Army was killed, and today you said that you absolutely did not see the killing itself. Which of that is true? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The truth is that we were prevented and that we could not see the murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. T, let me point out to you that you described the murder for the -- in a very detailed way in your first statement and you signed it. I can show you your signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I believe that this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me just add something to what I said you signed in your statement. Before you signed it, it is mentioned, and I quote, "I have nothing further to add to this. I have heard this statement being read back to me. I am prepared to repeat it before a Tribunal or any other international institution which may express an interest in it. Should I remember any additional details, I am prepared to amend the statement. I consider it my own and I confirm it by signing it." Do you understand me? You saw this written down when you were signing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you say that in spite of all of this, that this statement is not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The end of this story, that is until the murder itself, is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to add -- in October of 1992 you again went for the third time with Arif over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So in spite of all the dangers which you were exposed to, the first and the second time, you still went for a third time in that area. Mr. T, it would seem that Arif Delija and you, as members of the TO, were sent there to reconnoitre the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just another detail in relation to this statement. Yesterday you mentioned a soldier named Boban. This man is never mentioned in any of your statements, but a different person is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Ante Budimir is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Is that this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, his nickname was Bobi or Boban, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you told the Prosecutor yesterday that that was his real name. He asked you expressly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. I meant -- I thought that it was, because we have called him by that name throughout the time that I have known him since childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is not so important. You may have recalled yesterday I got up to object to the HDZ mention. Can we agree that you do not know very specific details about the HDZ organisation; that is, when it was established, who were the Presidents and so on? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Superficially I do know, but globally speaking, I don't know all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My question, Witness T, is that you do not know precisely in detail everything that I said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In other words, you know what the general knowledge was in Busovaca at the time; that's what you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But I need to ask you one thing regarding Mr. Kordic. Actually, a series of questions regarding Mr. Kordic. We've resolved the issue on the HDZ, so I'll skip that. But yesterday you said that Mr. Kordic was the vice-president of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who was the President of this war presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I believe that it was Asim Sunulahpasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Asim Sunulahpasic was President of the executive board in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know when this war presidency was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I believe in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have asked you better. What war presidency are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The joint one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So in fact you are not referring to the war presidency but to the joint crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the criteria according to which this joint crisis staff was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I know that there was parity in terms of the victory achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Sunulahpasic entered this crisis staff as President of the executive council, that is to say the then government of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know who at that time was President of the Municipal Assembly of Busovaca? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was from the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you don't know who it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me put a simpler question to you. Perhaps can you tell the Honourable Court on what you base your assertion that Mr. Kordic was vice-president. You are referring to this crisis staff, if we've -- clear that up today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you tell us some facts upon which you base your assertion? Actually, you are not sure, if that is how I can interpret your silence, that Mr. Kordic was vice-president to Mr. Sunulahpasic in this crisis staff, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I think that Kordic was commander of the Territorial Defence and then transferred to the post of vice-president of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I understand that that's what you think, but I asked you for the facts. By the way, who was Commander of the Territorial Defence? Husein Hadzimejlic, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it wasn't Mr. Kordic, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: But at one period of time he was present in this staff, Dario Kordic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was never in the Territorial Defence, Witness T. He was secretary in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The secretary for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, for national defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I know, but this is an executive agency, not a military agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, let me be quite frank about this. It is not my opinion; it is a fact.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The crisis staff was established -- that is to say the joint staff -- was established as follows. It was the president of the municipality and the president of the executive council, or the executive board, and a few other persons. The president of the municipal assembly was ex officio president of this joint crisis staff, if that's what we're going to call it, and the president of the executive board or executive counsel was the vice-president of this crisis staff. The name that you could not remember is the president of the municipal assembly of Busovaca, Mr. Zoran Maric. He was the president of the crisis staff, and his deputy was Mr. Asim Sunulahpasic, not Mr. Kordic. Obviously you had made a mistake. Do you agree with what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you can really get much further with this. There will be evidence which you can produce if you want on this particular topic. I think you have dealt very thoroughly with it as far as the witness is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just following your instructions from earlier on, that in such situations, we should present our own position quite clearly and then see what the witness will say to that. But perhaps we may proceed at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps another question related to the war presidency that was set up in Kacuni in January 1993, January. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know that the president of the war presidency -- I'm talking about the war presidency that was established by the Muslims in Kacuni -- was Asir Mekic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but this was after I got out of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, this was in January 1993, but never mind. If you don't know anything about this, I'm not going to put any further questions to you about it. Yesterday you said that Mr. Dario Kordic wore a uniform every now and then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today, on the photograph, you showed an armband on Mr. Kordic's left arm, as all other persons had, and it said "HVO"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, where did Mr. Kordic wear insignia of his rank?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps we could use the same photograph. With the permission of the Court, perhaps we could have the photograph placed on the ELMO once again. I think it is Z248,2B, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Where is his rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The rank was here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do we agree that it's not on this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. But here --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And when did you first see Mr. Kordic wearing a sign of his rank on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: In '92, in the month of July or August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When the HVO brigade was formed, the one you mentioned, in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just one more question related to this photograph, so let's sort that out. The caption --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The caption is not an integral part of the photograph, right? It is from a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This was written without any quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But we have to explain this to the Judges, because both you and I understand what this means, but we have to explain it to the Judges. So it says "Za Ka pe Dom spremni," "Prepared for the house of correction," "Kostroman, Kordic, Blaskic." Do we agree, Witness T, that "KP Dom" is an abbreviation for "house of correction"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So that means "prison," right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but it is also -- there is also another abbreviation there, and that is of "Za Dom spremni," "ready for the homeland."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, let's not quarrel on this, because these are two completely different things, "Ka pe Dom spremni" and "Za Dom spremni." Let us just explain this to the Judges. Let us just explain the source. Thank you. When you spoke of this act -- or rather when you spoke about rank, yesterday you said that you did not find the rank clear. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I did not know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But in your previous statement, you said that it was an officer's rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is to say a senior officer's rank, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But that is only your inference; you don't really know this for sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know, to the best of your knowledge, whether a single soldier in July 1992, or a single uniformed person in the HVO, had any rank, any sign of rank, on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You never saw anyone else? Thank you. To put this as briefly as possible, the part where you mentioned the Tisa Hotel, you spoke about a series of units that had their command, to the best of your knowledge, over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But I think we will agree that the MUP never had its headquarters in the Tisa Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The military police, the intervention platoon, et cetera, they had their headquarters where you mentioned, behind Nama, or rather behind the bus station? How shall I put it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but the intervention platoon was in Tisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Another piece of information related to Skorpions.
