utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We're talking about Mr. Dario Kordic all the time, so I'll tell you quite frankly that I never heard of that name. Who told you that they were called Skorpions? What do you base this conclusion upon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I base it on statements made by my friends, that part of the intervention platoon was involved in guarding Dario Kordic personally, and they were called Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So that is something you heard about in Busovaca; rumour had it in Busovaca that that's the way it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, yes, perhaps you could put it that way too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But we agree that the men we are talking about did not have any special insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No. No, they did not have any special insignia, except for their uniforms, their weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. Like any other soldier, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us continue with the questions related to Mr. Kordic, so that we could be as accurate as possible. Yesterday, in response to the Prosecutor's question, and it was a direct question, you were supposed to say, on the basis of your own experience, what your opinion was as to when Mr. Dario Kordic became president of the HDZ and whether he had any authority, and you answered that he had political authority in several municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: First of all, how do you know that, and what is that conclusion based upon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: It is based upon what was seen on television, on TV Busovaca. They broadcast live the sessions where these gentlemen were present and where they passed crucial decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, these were political discussions, political meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Military too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Give me one example when a military session was televised and when Mr. Kordic was present, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: '93, the month of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What was this meeting about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, it directly had to do with the exchange of territories and the moving out of Muslims from Zenica, Visoko, from Zenica to Vitez, then also marking borders, territories, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, that is from one of the articles that you gave us from these newspapers that you gave us. This is mentioned in one of the articles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, possibly. I didn't read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But may I, on the basis of what you said, conclude that you watched a press conference on television, not a military meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, the gentlemen were present there, the gentlemen from the military and political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But this was a press conference, for journalists from home and abroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, maybe. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. If we've agreed on that, then we can go on. Sorry, I forgot another question from that area. When you said "political authority," I don't want the Honourable Trial Chamber to misunderstand what we are saying, especially because all of this is being interpreted into the English language. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: In this situation of war in Busovaca, the political structures of government were absorbed, mobilised for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, you said that yesterday, that's correct, but in response to another question. However, your opinion was that Mr. Kordic had political power in all those municipalities that you mentioned. What do you mean by that? Because the Court should understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, persons who were dedicated to Dario Kordic were put in key positions. For example, an acquaintance of mine, Pasko Ljubicic, in the municipality of Vitez, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, when you're talking about these influences --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: -- actually, do you know who the president of the HVO was, after the HVO was established, of the civilian government of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I think it was Zoran Maric, the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: From the very outset, when the HVO was established, the HVO government; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But that's not correct, Mr. T. Florijan Glavocevic was the first president. You know Mr. Glavocevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: He was elected president of the Territorial Defence, too, on behalf of both populations. However, this was never established. The reasons were clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, we are talking about political influence, and in that context I'm asking you the following: Do you agree with me when I say that Florijan Glavocevic was the president of the civilian government of HVO in Busovaca before Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do we agree that the civilian government of the HVO had so-called administrative executive functions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is to say, in other words, it did the things that a municipality otherwise does?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but the military had priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you didn't answer my question as to how it was that Mr. Kordic had power in Fojnica, Stari Travnik, and for that matter, you mentioned all the surrounding municipalities. And if you just will wait for the interpretation to be finished.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I say that Pasko Ljubicic was a good acquaintance and a friend of Dubravka Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness T, you mentioned Pasko Ljubicic. I asked you about Travnik and Fojnica, that is the two towns in opposite ends of the region. And how did Mr. Kordic have authority power there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: He was seen during masses, in churches where he held speeches and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know about other municipalities: Kresevo, Kiseljak? Do you have any specific facts which you can mention or do you just conclude this in general from his political activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I know from Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you tell us any fact about the political influence of Mr. Kordic regarding the situation, let's say, in the municipality of Novi Travnik? And what is the basis of your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The forces which were sent to take Novi Travnik were sent from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now that you mention Busovaca, who was the HVO military commander in Busovaca at the time? Do you know? If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just mentioned the HDZ military structures in Busovaca xxx, and you said that Dusko Grubesic was a commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but this was in '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who was there before him, so that the Trial Chamber has a full picture of it? Who was the commander of the Busovaca brigade, that is, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, before Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness T, if you will agree with me, you make inferences on Mr. Kordic's political power based on his political activity, but that's just your inference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yesterday, I don't think that this was very relevant, but you brought it up, so I need to ask you. You said that Mr. Dario Kordic was related and on friendly terms with the Anto Sliskovic family because Franjo Sliskovic, Anto's brother, had married the sister of Mr. Kordic's wife; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you talked about these relations between Mr. Sliskovic and Kordic and when you mentioned all of this, you placed all this in the context of 1992, because that was the year that was being discussed at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness T, you obviously confused this with some other -- because of some other things, and I will say why, and I apologise to the Trial Chamber for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't follow this. Mr. Naumovski, what are you going to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just coming to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Franjo Sliskovic married the sister of Kordic's wife in December of 1994. That was much later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Well, that was only on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can prove it if necessary, but perhaps we should not dwell on this. But let me point to you to another matter. Yesterday you said expressly that Mr. Kordic was superior to Mr. Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you provided no fact to support it. Could you state any facts in that respect for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: The units which went to liberate Novi Travnik went from Busovaca through Nadioci, Ahmici, Vitez and beyond. These units were led by Dario Kordic. I say this on the basis of fact that he was stopped at the checkpoint at the limits of the Busovaca municipality by the reserve forces of MUP of Busovaca municipality -- that is, Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you give us the precise location where this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: This was between Nadioci and the restaurant called Sunce, where the road winds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So was that before the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: That was on the stretch before Nadioci and the Vitez municipality limits and Busovaca municipality limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: How do you know this? Who told you about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: My nephew, who was there at the checkpoint, he told me this. And later on, after the Ahmici were occupied, he was killed and massacred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's finish. That's your nephew, is it, who was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: It's a cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness T, I have to tell you that the Trial Chamber had an opportunity to hear other witnesses who claimed that Mr. Dario Kordic was at some meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a pure comment. You can make the comment to us. It's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just wanted to confront the witness with that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But I can put it to the witness that Mr. Kordic was never stopped at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, you can put it to me, but can you prove it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I am not here to answer your questions, but I will put it to you that there was no witness who testified here who testified to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us move on, Witness T. Yesterday you very specifically said that Mr. Kordic was a cousin of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I did not find that in the transcript, but I think that you even elucidated that it was on the maternal side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I thought that it was actually the paternal side, through his father, Pero Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not go deeper into that. But this is your opinion. Now, can you give us any fact to support it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: From conversations among the Croats in Busovaca, I reached that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand it correctly, those are some kind of rumours or stories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this may be irrelevant, but Mr. Kordic is not -- has no relation that was stated. I think that maybe something else was intended by such implication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just one detail regarding the Busovaca mosque. Are we in agreement that Mr. Kordic responded to a question by a journalist that, "Why shouldn't there be a mosque in Busovaca when there are mosques in other cities?" And he made a specific reference to Rome.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. He said that there was one in Rome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, on what day in the week was it when the conflict in Busovaca broke out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: It was -- I think it was Saturday or Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If it was Saturday or Sunday, then your dates are wrong, because the Sunday was the 24th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: So that would have been on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So then we would agree that it was a Monday, not on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We have already spoken about what had gone on a couple of days before, which was an attempt at abduction of Mr. Kostroman and Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today you mentioned that they were taken to the silo for a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what a silo was, what it meant at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: That was a place which was used by the Yugoslav People's Army, which was then turned over or was taken and given to use to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My very specific question was: Was that a camp for Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And when did it become a camp for Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I believe sometime in July or August, maybe even September 1993, but this -- but not that military complex. It was another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But where the silo was, in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do we agree that the day before the 25th, that is, on the 24th, at 3 p.m., two Croats were killed at the Kacuni checkpoint: Ivica Petrovic from Busovaca and another person who was from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you go to Kacuni on a regular basis before the conflict, that is throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: To Kacuni. I would say through Kacuni, yes, but to Kacuni only on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I had in mind a wider area of Kacuni with regard to your duties in defence activities throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When the Territorial Defence was deployed in Kacuni, it was meant by personnel mostly from Busovaca and the surrounding areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But on the days when that abduction -- when Ivica Petrovic and Igor Bogdanovic were killed, a number of soldiers from Zenica arrived there, that is, from the Zenica TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: At that time I did not go to the Kacuni area. I heard that some Croats were killed, that is, later, and that there was a conflict. And I had an opportunity to see this. And that there were some units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My apologies. It is not in the -- it is not -- it was not entered into the transcript that those two men were Croats who were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. And I heard that they were killed and that they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I think that that is corrected. We can move on. The day when the conflict started on the 25th of January 1993, Witness T, you were still a member of the TO and you had certain duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but that was later, I believe before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We are talking about the time period up to 25th of January?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before you go on. Now, how is this going to assist the Trial Chamber in deciding this case? Again, it seems to me an effort to establish that there was misconduct or there were murders of some Croats. Even if that is so, how does that justify what happened thereafter? Now, we need really to speed up. This witness has been giving evidence for a long time. We ought to try and finish him today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the situation is very simple. We assert that everything that preceded the conflict, and the Honourable Trial Chamber has already heard about this -- actually, we are going to prove this during our own case, that the Muslims attacked the Croats on the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will prove what is relevant, and not a series of allegations against the other side. You can prove what's relevant, but really the tit-for-tat approach is taking up a great deal of time. And I am speaking for myself. I am very concerned about it. Because I am not sure that it's relevant to these matters. In any event, can we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it please the Court. This is not a question of tit-for-tat. We are just trying to explain how the war in Busovaca broke out in January 1993 and who attacked who.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Witness T.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't mention '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Court knows about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Witness T, please don't intervene. Mr. Naumovski, will you now move along with this cross-examination and try and complete it so that if there is any other questions by Defence counsel, it can be altogether finished by the time the adjournment comes. You have been cross-examining for something like an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do bear time in mind and I believe that we are going to finish everything during the rest of the day today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As for this unit that was established in this area, Mr. T, just one more question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: -- this platoon that we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: -- that is to say, this military unit, had positioned itself on the hill of Crvencina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: This platoon was deployed in the zone of responsibility in the defence of Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, I am talking about you, who were in Busovaca at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I am also talking about the very same platoon, and I am saying that part of the platoon, not the entire platoon -- that is to say, 60 per cent -- with all their weapons, and all the other platoons from the detachment of Busovaca, were engaged in the defence of Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, part of the platoon was in Busovaca, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, but without any weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, it is no part of counsel's task to argue with the witnesses. Put your case, get the answer, and then please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question, Your Honour. Thank you. And I do apologise if I started arguing with the witness for a moment or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After the shooting and after the fighting that ensued, did you withdraw to Nezir Mujicic's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And that's where you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (redacted) mentioned Nermin Elezovic and Jasmin Sehovic's murders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I believe we will agree that it was others that told you about this; you were not there, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: (redacted). We were taken out together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But you did not see the actual killing; that's what I am trying to say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to shorten the proceedings, so I'm not going to put any other questions in this respect, but I wish to draw your attention to D38/1, which speaks of this incident, so I don't really have to question the witness about this unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, I have to go back to this document, the one that you gave from the newspapers, that is to say, Z248/2. You were in the army, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could this please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So that is the document that we discussed today, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you were in the army, and you know that such secret documents, so to speak, have in their upper right-hand corner a sign saying "Confidential," "Strictly Confidential," or "Military Secret," or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you say yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This document doesn't have that, does it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the sentence that you could not read, at the very bottom, the last sentence in this paper is: "Members of the HVO who resist should be disarmed, and in more serious incidents, killed." Is that what you could not have read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the last thing , something that we have here in the Croatian text, that is to say the order for an attack on Travnik. At the very bottom, that is a headline from a newspaper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today a document was shown to you, 861, or rather the other one, that pertains to your neighbour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it's 861,1. Do you agree with me that in these documents, no specific time is mentioned? It doesn't say at any point how long this is valid, for how long a period is this valid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you had this same kind of document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but a different nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But, please, why did you state in your earlier statements that you did have a limit, a time limit, on your document, the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps I referred to the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So perhaps it's a mistake; do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to finish as soon as possible, so I'm trying to see what are the new things that he mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. T, do you agree that in the period -- or rather in the summer of 1993, to be precise, before you left Busovaca, there was a big wave, so to speak, of refugees from Travnik in this entire region; they came to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity of seeing that at the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today, Mr. T, you presented an opinion of yours that Mr. Dario Kordic had to know about everything that was going on in Busovaca. That is your conclusion, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness T, did you ever see Mr. Kordic say in public or write in public or sign in public a military order for an attack against the Muslims? I'm referring to the period from May 1992 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: No. Personally, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So your conclusion is based on what we would call general knowledge, or rumour? I don't know if you understand what I'm saying. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I think, Witness T, that we're almost over with my questions. Let me just have a look and see whether I've missed something. I'm going to change this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps, for the very end -- well, perhaps it's best for me to finish at this point, Your Honours. I'm afraid that if I put another question, I'm going to enter a new subject altogether, so then I'm going to be short for time. I thank you once again, and I thank you, Witness, for your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, you've got a few minutes left. If you want to go into something else, of course, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't think that you prevented me from carrying out my work. I just think that I should finish at this point because I'm afraid I should not raise any other issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know the answer, Your Honour: No, we don't have any questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't always be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two questions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness T, in relation to the group that you have called the Skorpions, were any of those Skorpions known to you by name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: They were part of the intervention platoon. The intervention platoon consisted of troublesome Croats, who were wanted men by the police and things like that. That is to say that before the conflict, they had done things they were not supposed to do. As for the names, I personally met Milenko Akrap; I knew him from before. Ivica Kristo. Ivica from Gusti Grab; I cannot remember the name right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you there. Where did you get the name "Skorpion" from? Did you get it from talking to people you knew, or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: They said, either by way of a joke or not, on the 17th of April 1993, in front of the department store in Busovaca -- actually, in that part of the street, I mean, I was there for medical reasons; I was walking along that street. I reached that street where the intervention platoon, the military police, had some kind of a celebration. It so happened that I was stopped, and I was forced to drink beer with them to celebrate some kind of victory. Among others, Drazen Kresic, Dzare Pulic were there, and other acquaintances who knew me. They were friendly towards me, and as we talked and joked, they said that they belonged to the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Second question: How short or long a time after the alleged stopping of Kordic at the checkpoint did your relation, your nephew or your cousin, report that to you? So how long after the stopping was it that he told you about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: Some 30 days went by; that is, from when he was stopped at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I guess it was at night. I believe this checkpoint then pulled back to the cemetery below Ahmici, and during that night --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I want to know. There is a third question, and it's this. Your visits to the area of Tisovac, just answer this question if you want to: Were they part of an act of reconnoitring, or were they just pastime, or do you prefer not to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T [resumed]:
utterances.text: I say with responsibility that I did not go there as part of any military tasks; that I went to the area of Tisovac -- even before the war, I engaged in fishing, I went to get mushrooms, and other activities that had some economic value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness T, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released. While these matters are being looked into, Mr. Nice, you've got one witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the moment I have an embarrassment in relation to witnesses which I am finding out about, and I'll tell you about it when this witness withdraws.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we pass from this witness, in my efforts to be economic with time and with paper, I think I've probably been nothing but confusion and difficulty to your staff. And it occurs to me that in relation to the newspaper, it might be prudent to have the four extracts from the newspaper, which are four sheets, collectively produced as a separate exhibit, because it may be that the accuracy of one of the other orders in comparison with the orders already proved will come to be of significance; it may be not. They are four sheets, and they could be produced as a single exhibit, 2783, and the Chamber will then know that the whole newspaper was copied for the Defence. But I think I've rather caused problems with the numbering; I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could discuss that with the registry to find the most convenient answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position as to the witnesses is, to say the least, worrying. I think the last week and this week, the problems we've faced with three major witnesses booked to attend on either last week, this week, and next week, whatever it is, include such things as a witness being quite willing to attend and then at the last minute finding that his son was going to visit him in a far-off land, unknown to him, and his then saying, "I'm not coming"; a witness, having been booked a long time in advance, coming from the other side of the world, when we tried to reorganise the schedule to make things fit, he is entirely unavailable, and so we can't yet be sure whether he is coming as planned or not, and he's a high-ranking officer, who is only going to give us a very limited amount of time; and then the witness that I -- I didn't identify; was identified very helpfully for me last week as somebody who could fill what was by now becoming a short week, a witness who is in the building and I had thought was going to be available to give evidence tomorrow, I've just received a message, which is why Mr. Scott's left the room, that unknown to us, though he very helpfully came for the last two days, he may not now be available tomorrow, so I am investigating that at once. These witnesses are all, I think, military or similar witnesses. And looking ahead to next week in general, there is a problem that we're going to have too little evidence, or it may be, if the witness who comes from the other side of the world arrives, because he has been booked and is going to come and that's that, and he's only going to give us two days, we may have too much evidence. What I would ask in relation to these, as it were, professional witnesses is that if necessary, consideration be given to the possibility of their summaries counting as, once adopted, evidence, save and to the extent that the Defence identify passages that need to be taken in detail and could be the subject of cross-examination. Of course, it may be, rather than having too much evidence, that I shall land up having too little. As to tomorrow, I'm going to need a few minutes yet to find out what the position is. As you will understand, I've sent a message out immediately asking the colonel whether he can do anything to rearrange tomorrow's appointment, of which we were earlier unaware, and be available to help us with evidence tomorrow. That's Mr. Schipper. I know the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: What is the situation, now? What is the situation, exactly? That you have no witness for tomorrow morning, or maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as of ten minutes ago, I was told no. Mr. Scott's gone out to attempt negotiations, but I understand that it is a firm no. He is a military officer from northern Europe, and he apparently is intent on returning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have no more witnesses from now to the end of this week at least?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: And you are not sure about the next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next week I think I have two or three witnesses. If it's two witnesses, it will be a bit too little; if it's three witnesses, given that they are substantial witnesses, it could be a little bit too much. I have erred on the side of having too many witnesses, and I have attempted to make arrangements to have the witness coming from the other side of the world come, on the basis that I forecast the Chamber would probably prefer to accommodate that arrangement rather than the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, so it's important that we get on with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Despite these difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last week and the next week have proved to be quite extraordinarily difficult. There have been earlier problems that have had a knock-on effect of changes in the Trial Chamber's timetable and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And there will be further?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There will be further ones like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can tell you now that because of the requirements of another case, we shall not be sitting in the afternoons of the 24th and 25th, so that week will be shortened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Incidentally, I know that this witness would be available this afternoon. I think we raise that because if yesterday's position had continued, that might have been a possibility, but I can recognise that that will no longer be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not, because of the requirements of the other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. I think I've said before, the arrangement of witnesses is extremely difficult, and we are working flat out to find people at all times, and this is I think the first time we have run into a serious block. But unless my discussions with the colonel are going to have any more results than Mr. Scott's, and I can see no reason to believe that's likely to be the case, it looks as though we are out of witnesses for tomorrow. There's the argument about the one dead witness; that in itself I don't think will take much longer to argue, because it's been argued substantially already, and there is a limited amount of outstanding discussion; and in any event, that argument, although it can be self-contained, has a connection with some evidence yet to come. For example -- let me just explain that. The evidence that we seek to adduce relates to a sighting of Kordic on the night before the attack in Donje Veceriska. There is evidence of another witness dealing in some detail with earlier sightings of Mr. Kordic at the same place -- not on that particular night, but going to show a pattern of visits. And of course that would be either corroborative material or similar-fact material, or material of some weight, to support the evidence that will be coming from the statement of the deceased, so that even arguing about it might not lead to its ultimate resolution because the Chamber might prefer to make a resolution of that issue after hearing the evidence of the other visits to Donje Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would seem sensible to leave that argument until that evidence has been heard. Very well. How long do you want, as it were, to find out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could give me about ten minutes, I'll go and speak to the man directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we shall do is to adjourn, and if you find that you can call the witness tomorrow, will you kindly let us have word by quarter past 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Otherwise this matter is adjourned until Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: What do you aim for Monday morning? What is the programme?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Personally, I shall be here on Monday morning, but the balance of next week I have to attend on the other Chamber for another trial. But on Monday morning it's going to be, I hope, a man called Carter, and I think he is now definitely arriving, and the alternative is it will be Brigadier -- or he may now be General Duncan. But I think he is probably going to come next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: If you have the summary ready before the end of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any summaries that are prepared will be made available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the problem, again -- I'm running into an objection, I think, or a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few brief comments, Mr. President. First, we have some matters of a legal nature that we wanted to raise with the Trial Chamber, and I had thought that they were going to be addressed tomorrow. I would not anticipate that they would take more than an hour in total. With respect to the second matter regarding the deceased witness, that's an issue which has been lying fallow for a long time. And we've heard for the first time today that apparently the theory is that this is going to -- even though there are no corroborative witnesses for this particular piece of evidence, there is going to be evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct, supposedly. Well, I would suggest that that's subject to Rule 93 concerns, Rule 93(b) concerns, and I do not believe any disclosures of an allegation of such a consistent pattern of conduct have been made to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are the matters you want to raise? Just give me an idea in a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, there was an issue relating to the current protective order, which perhaps needs to be expanded. There's an issue related to the confidential witnesses that have been brought before the Chamber so far who have -- for whom protections have been sought, and only to recant the necessity of those protections when they actually take the stand. And I'm sure that the Trial Chamber can appreciate the extremely difficult position in which that puts the Defence. There are also some other relatively discreet issues. I thought we were going to address the issue of dead witnesses generally, Your Honour, and that raises the Aleksovski appeal decision concerns. I don't believe that it's a particularly complicated legal argument, maybe Mr. Nice disagrees, but it's something that should be addressed sooner rather than later. Things of that variety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will sit to hear the matters that the Defence wish to raise, but it may well be that we will not hear the argument about the dead witnesses for the reasons which Mr. Nice has already alluded to. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if we are going to sit tomorrow in any event, I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he is available, I take it the Chamber would rather have evidence tomorrow. I'll communicate with somebody in the appropriate department and let you know one way or the other what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of November, 1999, at 9.30 a.m.
